pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 7–9, Weather vs Climate — weather is what the atmosphere is doing now/today (changes hour to hour); climate is the typical long-term pattern of weather in a place averaged over many years.
• Standards — UK (DfE): the distinction sits across KS1/KS2 science (Y1 Seasonal changes) and KS2 geography (hot/cold areas relative to Equator and poles; climate zones).
• Standards — US (NGSS): 3-ESS2-1 'represent data… [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-ESS2-1]' (note: assessment boundary excludes climate change) and 3-ESS2-2 '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-ESS2-2]'. State/regional tier DEFERRED.
• Operational details: teach the difference as a matter of TIMESCALE and AGGREGATION — climate is the long-run average, weather is a single sample; use the maxim 'climate is what you expect, weather is what you get'; build from many days of real weather data settling into a stable average; directly pre-empt the 'a cold day disproves warming' conflation (kept age-appropriate, not full climate-change teaching).
• Checkpoint (Tier A|B|C): Tier A — sort statements as weather or climate and give an example showing one cold day doesn't change the climate; Tier B — explain climate as a multi-year average and compare two places; Tier C — reason about trends vs variability and why single events are weak evidence.
bestPractices: Use the anchor phrase 'climate is what you expect, weather is what you get' and return to it repeatedly
Show aggregation directly: accumulate many days of a place's weather and watch a running average settle into its climate band — make the timescale visible
Contrast two places with the same day's weather but different climates to separate the single sample from the long-run pattern
Explicitly address the misconception that one unusually cold (or hot) day changes or disproves the climate/trend
Keep climate-change specifics light at this age per the 3-ESS2-1 assessment boundary — focus on the weather/climate distinction itself
keyRepresentations: A scatter of daily weather points with a running-average line settling into a stable climate band
A wide vs narrow time-window slider (few days = weather, many years = climate)
Side-by-side 'today' snapshot vs 'typical year' summary for the same place
A sorting mat: statements dropped into WEATHER vs CLIMATE columns
commonMisconceptions: 'A cold day (or snowstorm) means the climate isn't warming' — confusing one weather sample with the long-term trend
Weather and climate are synonyms / interchangeable words
Climate is just 'the weather somewhere far away or exotic' rather than the long-run average of any place's weather
Climate never changes / weather is totally random — both are patterns at different timescales

learn.summary: For ages 7–9, distinguish weather (what the atmosphere is doing now/today, changeable hour to hour) from climate (the typical long-run pattern of weather in a place, averaged over many years — roughly 30). The core idea is TIMESCALE and AGGREGATION: climate is the long-run average, weather is a single sample. Use the anchor phrase 'climate is what you expect, weather is what you get', build climate from many days of real weather data settling into a stable average, and directly address the belief that one unusually cold (or hot) day changes or disproves the climate. Keep climate-change specifics light at this age, focusing on the weather/climate distinction itself.

activities.title: Watch a climate form from many days of weather
feedback: If a learner says the climate changed when the freezing day was added, point them back to the running-average line: ask how far it actually moved compared to how far a single point jumped.
If a learner calls the narrow few-day window 'climate', ask them how many years of data the window is covering, and whether a handful of days can reveal the typical pattern.
When the second town forms a different band from its own weather, ask: could both towns have the same weather on one day but still have these different climates? (Yes.)
Reinforce with the anchor phrase: 'climate is what you expect, weather is what you get'.
activities.rationale: The concept is aggregation across a timescale, which becomes concrete when learners accumulate samples and watch a running average settle. Making the running mean and an adjustable time window visible turns the abstract 'long-term average' into something a child can watch form, and the single record-day demonstration targets the trend-vs-sample misconception directly. Swapping to a second town extends this to comparing climates in different regions — a different place averages its own weather into a different stable band.
sourceClaims: A persistent public/student misconception conflates a single cold-weather event with the long-term climate trend; climate is best framed as the multi-year average pattern of weather.
learnerActions: Step forward through a town's daily weather, one day at a time — a jittery mix of hot and cold days plotted as daily temperature points (rain can be tracked on a separate chart).
Watch a running-average line gradually settle into a steady band as more and more days accumulate.

Narrow a time window to just a few days and describe what you see (scattered, hard to predict = WEATHER); widen it to many years and describe how the long-run average and the usual seasonal pattern become steady and predictable (= CLIMATE).
Drop in one unusually freezing record-day and watch how much (or how little) the many-year average moves.
Switch to a second town and watch a different climate band form from its own weather, then compare the two towns' climates.
Say out loud, in your own words, why one cold day does not change the climate.
activities.intendedInsight: Climate is the long-run average of many days of weather; a single day is just one sample, so one cold or hot day barely shifts the multi-year average and cannot by itself tell you the climate.

activities.title: Today vs a typical year, side by side
feedback: If a learner treats the two panels as the same kind of thing, ask which one could change by tomorrow and which would stay roughly the same for years.
Prompt for the timescale: climate needs many years (about 30) of averaged data, not a single day.
activities.rationale: A side-by-side snapshot-vs-summary comparison states the distinction clearly and supports learners who are not ready to reason about an accumulating average. It is a scaffold: it labels the difference and presents a 'typical year' summary of conditions, but does not itself show the aggregation over time that drives the concept, so it works best as a lead-in to or support for the accumulating-average activity.
sourceClaims: NGSS 3-ESS2-1: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-ESS2-1]'; assessment boundary explicitly does not include climate change.
learnerActions: Look at a 'today' snapshot for a place (one day's weather) next to a 'typical year' summary for the same place.
Reveal labels and state which panel shows weather and which shows climate, and why.
Explain what you would need to collect — and over how long — to describe the climate of your own town.
activities.intendedInsight: Weather is a single-day snapshot of the atmosphere; climate is a summary of the typical pattern built from many years of such snapshots.

activities.title: Sort statements: weather or climate?
feedback: For the trap item, if a learner says one hot day shows the climate is warming, respond: that is weather — one day's state of the atmosphere; climate is the average over many years, so a single day cannot show the trend.
If a learner sorts 'It is raining right now' as climate, ask whether that statement could be true today and false tomorrow — if so, it is weather.
Model the correct example: a desert can have a rainy day and still have a desert climate, because its climate is the average over many years.
activities.rationale: A categorization task plus a targeted trap item maps closely onto the teaching objective — sorting weather vs climate and testing the trend-vs-sample misconception. This is a recognition/categorization format, so it can check whether the learner applies the distinction but does not by itself elicit an extended independent explanation; pair it with a spoken or written justification to capture reasoning.
sourceClaims: A persistent public/student misconception conflates a single cold-weather event with the long-term climate trend; climate is best framed as the multi-year average pattern of weather.
learnerActions: Drag or write statements into two columns, WEATHER and CLIMATE (e.g. 'It is raining right now', 'Summers here are usually hot and dry', 'It snowed yesterday', 'This region is hot all year round').
Answer a trap item: a single record-hot (or record-cold) day — does that one day change the climate? Choose and justify.
Give your own example that shows one cold day doesn't change the overall climate.
activities.intendedInsight: Deciding whether each statement is about a single moment or a long-run average checks that the learner separates a single sample from the aggregated pattern, including rejecting the claim that one extreme day changes the climate.

activities.title: Question a climate expert about a cold snap
feedback: If a learner accepts the cold snap as proof, restate: one day is weather; to say anything about climate you need long-run averages and trends.
Affirm that two towns can share one day's weather yet differ in climate, and that a desert staying a desert through a rainy day shows climate is the long-run average.
activities.rationale: A question-and-answer exchange can directly target the key 'one cold day' misconception and give practice articulating reasoning. Discussion can clarify the distinction, while the accumulating-average activity more directly shows the aggregation intuition; the two are complementary rather than interchangeable.
sourceClaims: A persistent public/student misconception conflates a single cold-weather event with the long-term climate trend; climate is best framed as the multi-year average pattern of weather.
learnerActions: Pose the question: 'Today there's a sudden cold snap — is that proof there's no warming?' and predict the answer before reading the reply.
Discuss follow-ups: 'Could two towns have the same weather today but different climates?' and 'A desert has a rainy day — has its climate stopped being a desert climate?'
Summarise, in your own words, what evidence would actually tell us about a place's climate.
activities.intendedInsight: Single weather events are weak evidence about climate; describing climate requires many years of averaged data and attention to trends, not individual days.

constraints: Target age 7–9; keep climate-change specifics light, consistent with the NGSS 3-ESS2-1 assessment boundary that excludes climate change — focus on the weather/climate distinction itself.

The side-by-side 'today vs typical year' snapshot is a scaffold: it labels the distinction but does not show aggregation over time, which is the heart of the concept. Use it to introduce or support, not as the whole lesson.

The sorting/categorization and multiple-choice formats are recognition tasks: they can check whether a learner applies the distinction but do not by themselves elicit extended independent explanation. Pair them with spoken or written justification.
State climate as roughly a 30-year average of weather for this age; avoid implying climate never changes or that weather is purely random — both are patterns at different timescales.

Interaction examples (daily-weather scatter, running-average line, time-window slider, dropping in a record day, swapping towns) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory features.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two NGSS citations are marked verified in the source row; the NOAA/NASA weather-vs-climate misconception claim is marked unverified — treat the misconception framing as plausible but not independently confirmed here.

The source's '3D adds nothing / would distract' and 'more powerfully shown than discussed' judgements are catalog fit opinions, not established efficacy findings; the conversation activity is retained here as a legitimate complementary approach rather than dismissed.
The 'about 30 years' figure for climate averaging comes from the assessment field; it is a standard convention but stated here as approximate for young learners.

The source 'climate is exotic/faraway weather' misconception is carried in the audit as an acknowledged source item but is not directly targeted by any proposed activity; a sorting item or discussion prompt about an ordinary local place could be added to address it.

The source 'climate is just whatever season it is right now' misconception is an explicit source error pattern (with a reteach prerequisite) but is likewise not directly targeted by any proposed activity; a seasonal sort item (e.g. 'It is cold this week' vs 'Winters here are usually mild') or a discussion prompt could add coverage.

NGSS 3-ESS2-1 is attached to the 'today vs typical year' activity as support for representing typical weather conditions; it concerns weather representation and explicitly excludes climate change, so it supports the 'typical conditions' representation rather than the multi-year-average definition itself — not independently re-verified.
Self-audit: no arithmetic or force/motion content to verify; the aggregation logic (a single sample barely moves a large multi-year mean) is sound as presented.

probeDeeper: What would you need to collect to describe the climate of your town — and over how long?
Could two towns have the same weather today but different climates? How?
A desert has a rainy day. Has its climate stopped being a desert climate? Why not?
assess.correctAnswer: No — one warm day is weather, the day-to-day state of the atmosphere. Climate is the average pattern of weather over many years (about 30). To say anything about climate you need long-run averages and trends, not a single day.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'It was hot/cold today, so climate change is/isn't real' — treats one day's weather as proof about climate
errorPatterns.nextMove: Put one day beside a 30-year average graph — show one point can't reveal the trend.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — a warm day shows the climate is getting warmer.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: cites a single day to confirm or deny climate change

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Weather and climate are the same thing, just different words'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Define weather as today's state, climate as the multi-year average of weather.
errorPatterns.distractor: There's no real difference; they both just mean what it's like outside.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Climate is just whatever season it is right now'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare a place's climate across all seasons averaged over many years.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: equates climate with the current season

responseLevels.gap: Uses today's weather to judge climate; treats the two terms as synonyms.
responseLevels.full: Rejects the one-day claim, defines climate as the multi-year average pattern of weather, and applies the distinction to a new case such as a rainy day in a desert or two same-weather towns with different climates.
responseLevels.partial: States weather is short-term and climate is long-term but still slips into citing single events, or can't say climate needs many years of averaged data.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: One December morning it is unusually warm where you live. Your friend says, 'See — that proves the climate is changing.' Is one warm day good evidence about climate? Explain what would actually tell us about the climate.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who conflates weather and climate reads any single hot or cold day as evidence about climate; only a child holding the timescale distinction rejects the one-day claim and asks for many years of averaged data.
